title: Block close: many rooms
hookLine: the family disagrees, and still says one creed

cards: A family can share one house and still argue about the thermostat, the dishes, whose turn it is to cook.

Through this whole block of the path, the Christian family has been arguing out loud: about the table, about Mary, about the saints, about images and the dead. No church here was asked to back down, and none did.
And yet the Nicene Creed, said in Orthodox, Catholic and other churches, still opens with the same words: I believe in one God. Today the block closes.

teach.b: This block asked the big questions, and let each church answer in its own voice. It began with words about God: theology, and the way of not-knowing that says what God is not.
It asked where authority lives, sola scriptura, scripture alone, or scripture read within the church's tradition, and what it means to call scripture God-breathed.
It tried pictures of the Trinity that all fall short, and the filioque, one word in a long argument.

Then sin and grace: Augustine and Pelagius, the Reformed comfort of being chosen, Wesley's grace that goes before. The cross from several sides: victory over death, a debt paid, a place taken, a love that changes us.
Justified by faith. Made holy. Theosis, becoming like God, iron glowing in the fire.

teach.h: THE CHURCH, ITS WATER AND TABLE.
teach.b: Then the church itself: its marks, its ministers, its water and its table. Mary, the God-bearer. The saints, the images, the dead.
Heaven, hell, and the promise of his return. The answers differed, and this block didn't pretend otherwise.
But listen to Jesus on his last night, praying for everyone who would believe through his friends: "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee."
And earlier that same evening, to friends who were frightened: "In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you." Mansions, in the King James. Dwelling places.
Rooms. Many of them, in one house, and room enough for a family that argues.

how: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches say the Nicene Creed in their worship, and Christians of different churches pray together, especially in shared services for Christian unity.

o: a street of churches standing side by side
a shut church door after the evening service
the last lesson of a stretch, looking back

games.q: words from this block — tap the pairs.

s: the King James says "many rooms" in John 14:2
it says "many mansions": dwelling places, rooms.
the churches in this block disagree about the table, Mary and the saints
and the creed they say still begins: I believe in one God.

games.q: it's Jesus's last night with his friends. he prays for them, and for everyone who will believe through them. what does he ask?
o: that they all may be one.
that they never meet anyone different.
games.why: "that they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee." a prayer for a family that would come to disagree.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose faith isn't yours: a Christian from another church, a neighbor from another tradition, a friend who holds no faith.

Don't think about where you disagree; think about their face, their week, what they might be carrying. If you pray, ask good things for them in words your tradition gives you; if you don't, wish them peace, warmly.

wordCard.voice: Block close. The end of the big questions: many answers, honestly different, from one family that still says one creed. Tomorrow a new block begins: traditions of prayer.

orig.note: Greek: a dwelling place, a place to stay; the word behind "mansions" in John 14:2.

carryVoice: Your line: many rooms, one house. I believe in one God, still said together. See you tomorrow.
